claims.text: (A^2)_ii equals the degree of n_i, so it is positive for every non-isolated vertex, while no path (distinct vertices) of length 2 starts and ends at n_i. On the board graph (A^2)_11 = 1, (A^2)_22 = 2, (A^2)_33 = 1; the only length-2 closed walks are n1 n2 n1, n2 n1 n2, n2 n3 n2, n3 n2 n3. Supersedes base claim C7.

support.quote: The number of walks of length 2 from a vertex to itself is just the number of edges at that vertex, or the vertex degree.

claims.text: Walk counting for a simple graph: for k >= 1, (A^k)_ij is the number of walks of length k from n_i to n_j. The paper proves it by induction on k, with base case k = 1 and step (A^(k+1))_ij = sum_r (A^k)_ir A_rj, grouping walks by their last-but-one vertex n_r. The textbook contains no such theorem (C8).

support.quote: Let k be a positive integer. Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix A^k is the number of walks of length k from v_i to v_j in G.
For any j, k ∈ [n] and ℓ ∈ N, there are A^ℓ_jk walks of length ℓ from j to k.
Then for any two vertices i and j, the entry (A^k)_ij counts the number of walks of length k from vertex i to vertex j.

claims.text: A^k counts walks, not paths, off the diagonal as well: on the board graph (A^3)_12 = 2, counted by the walks n1 n2 n1 n2 and n1 n2 n3 n2, and neither is a path nor a trail, and no path of length 3 joins n1 to n2 because a path in a 3-vertex graph has length at most 2.

support.quote: counts walks — not paths. This is because matrix multiplication accumulates all sequences of edges between two vertices, including those that revisit vertices and edges.
any path from u to v must have length ≤ n − 1, where n is the number of vertices of G (since a path of length k has k + 1 distinct vertices, but G has only n vertices to spare).

claims.text: Convention of this paper: a walk of length 0 (a single vertex) is allowed, so A^0 = I counts it and the theorem holds for k >= 0; the textbook is silent on length 0 and Grinberg allows it. This is the paper's own convention, not the textbook's.

support.quote: A walk (in G) means a finite sequence (v0 , v1 , . . . , vk ) of vertices of G (with k ≥ 0) such that all of v0 v1 , v1 v2 , v2 v3 , . . . , vk−1 vk are edges of G.

claims.text: A^k is symmetric for every k >= 0 when G is undirected: reversing a walk from n_i to n_j gives a walk from n_j to n_i of the same length, and this is a bijection. (Equivalently, the transpose of a product reverses the factors and A equals its transpose.)
